Joice, I read your report. It was very good. Can I ask you some questions?
Of course. Please, slowly.
Where did you go last month?
I went to four public schools, all in the east of São Paulo.
And who did you talk to in the schools?
I talked to the teachers and to two directors. I did not talk to the students.
Why did you choose those four schools?
Because they used the platform every day. The other schools did not.
That makes sense. And how did you organize the visits?
That is a very good question. I did not organize them alone. My colleague helped me.
Who did you meet at the conference?
Why did you choose this subject?
How did you prepare?
That is a very good question. I do not have the data here.

Hello. Today we have five questions for Marina Alves. What did you study in your project? Where did you go last year? When did the project start? Why did you choose small schools? And how did you prepare for the visits? Marina answered all of them in the newsletter, and her last answer is the most interesting: she read every report of the last ten years, and then she asked the teachers. Please read the interview before our call. Thank you.

Hi, this is a short message about the questions after your presentation. People usually ask three things. First, where the data comes from. Second, how many schools you visited. And third, why you chose this subject. You do not need a long answer. Two sentences are enough for each question. If somebody asks something you do not know, say: that is a very good question, I do not have the data here. Nobody expects more. Good luck in November.

Joice reads the interview with Marina in the newsletter. She writes three questions for the next meeting. She asks Marina where she went last year. She asks why Marina chose small schools. She writes the answers in her notebook.
